title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: Bounties

In Great Britain, particular branches of domestic industry frequently petition for export bounties, and sometimes they are granted. Supposedly these bounties let our merchants and manufacturers sell their goods as cheaply as their foreign rivals, or even cheaper. A larger quantity will then be exported, the argument runs, so the balance of trade tilts further in our favour. We cannot give our workers a monopoly abroad the way we have given them one at home. We cannot force foreigners to buy their goods the way we have forced our own countrymen to. So the next best plan, people have decided, is to pay foreigners for buying. This is how the mercantile system proposes to enrich the whole country and put money in everyone's pocket by working on the balance of trade.

Everyone agrees that bounties should go only to those branches of trade that cannot survive without them. But any branch in which the merchant can sell his goods at a price that returns his whole invested capital plus the ordinary profit can clearly survive without a bounty. Such a branch stands on exactly the same footing as every other trade carried on without bounties, so it needs one no more than they do. The only trades that require bounties are those where the merchant has to sell his goods for a price that does not return his capital plus the ordinary profit, or where he has to sell them for less than they actually cost to bring to market. The bounty is meant to cover that loss and to persuade him to keep going, or perhaps even to start, a trade whose costs are assumed to be greater than its returns, where every transaction eats up part of the capital invested in it, and which is of such a kind that if every other trade were like it, the country would soon have no capital left.

Notice that the trades carried on by means of bounties are the only ones that can be run between two nations for any length of time in such a way that one of them always and steadily loses, selling its goods for less than it cost to bring them to market. If the bounty did not repay the merchant what he would otherwise lose on the price of his goods, his own self-interest would soon force him to put his capital to some other use, or to find a trade in which the price returned his capital plus the ordinary profit. The effect of bounties, like that of every other device of the mercantile system, can only be to force a country's trade into a channel far less advantageous than the one it would naturally flow into on its own.

The clever and well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has shown very clearly that, since the bounty on corn exports was first set up, the value of the corn exported—valued at a fairly low rate—has exceeded the value of the corn imported—valued very high—by far more than the total of all the bounties paid over that period. On the true principles of the mercantile system, he takes this as clear proof that this forced corn trade benefits the nation, since the value of exports surpasses that of imports by far more than the whole extra public expense of getting the corn exported. What he overlooks is that this extra expense, the bounty itself, is the smallest part of what exporting corn really costs society. The capital the farmer used to grow it must also be counted in. Unless the price of the corn, when sold in foreign markets, returns not only the bounty but this capital plus the ordinary profit on it, society loses the difference, and the national stock shrinks by that much. Yet the very reason a bounty was thought necessary is that the price was assumed to be too low to do this.

It has been claimed that the average price of corn has fallen considerably since the bounty was established. I have already tried to show that the average price of corn began to fall somewhat towards the end of the last century and has gone on falling through the first sixty-four years of this one. But if this fall is real—and I believe it is—it must have happened in spite of the bounty, not because of it. The same fall has occurred in France as well as in England, even though France had no bounty at all and, until 1764, generally banned corn exports outright. So this gradual fall in the average price of grain is probably owing in the end to neither regulation, but to that gradual, imperceptible rise in the real value of silver which, in the first book of this work, I tried to show has taken place across the general market of Europe during this century. It seems altogether impossible that the bounty could ever help to lower the price of grain.

As I have already pointed out, in years of plenty the bounty triggers extra exports and so necessarily holds the home price of corn above the level to which it would otherwise sink. That was the openly stated aim of setting it up. In years of scarcity the bounty is often suspended, yet the heavy exporting it causes in years of plenty must often stop, to some degree, one year's surplus from relieving another year's shortage. So in both kinds of year the bounty necessarily tends to push the money price of corn somewhat higher in the home market than it would otherwise be.

I do not think any reasonable person will dispute that, given the actual state of farming, the bounty must have this effect. But many people have believed it encourages tillage, and in two ways. First, by opening a wider foreign market to the farmer's corn, they imagine it raises the demand for that crop, and so its production. Second, by guaranteeing the farmer a better price than he could otherwise expect in the present state of farming, they suppose it encourages tillage. This double encouragement, they imagine, must over a long stretch of years bring about such an increase in corn production that its home price falls far more than the bounty raises it, given whatever state farming has reached by the end of that period.

My answer is that whatever widening of the foreign market the bounty can produce must, in any given year, come entirely at the expense of the home market. Every bushel of corn exported because of the bounty, which would not have been exported without it, would otherwise have stayed in the home market, raising consumption and lowering the price of corn there. Notice that the corn bounty, like every other export bounty, imposes two separate taxes on the people. First, the tax they must pay to fund the bounty. Second, the tax that comes from the raised price of corn in the home market—and since everyone buys corn, in this particular commodity that tax is paid by the whole population. With corn, this second tax is by far the heavier of the two. Suppose that, year in and year out, the bounty of 5 shillings on each exported quarter of wheat raises the home price of wheat by only 6 pence a bushel, or 4 shillings a quarter above what it would have been given the actual crop. Even on this very modest assumption, the great body of the people, on top of paying the tax that funds the 5-shilling bounty on every exported quarter, must pay another 4 shillings on every quarter they consume themselves. But according to the very well-informed author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade, the corn exported amounts on average to no more than one part in thirty-one of what is consumed at home. So for every 5 shillings they pay towards the first tax, they must pay £6 4s towards the second. So heavy a tax on the first necessity of life must either cut into the food of the labouring poor, or raise their money wages in step with the higher money cost of their subsistence. To the extent that it works the first way, it reduces the poor's ability to educate and raise their children, and so tends to hold back the country's population. To the extent that it works the second way, it reduces employers' ability to employ as many of the poor as they otherwise could, and so tends to hold back the country's industry. So the extra corn exports caused by the bounty not only shrink the home market in any given year just as much as they widen the foreign one, but, by restraining the country's population and industry, in the end stunt the gradual growth of the home market itself—and thereby, over the long run, tend to shrink rather than enlarge the total market and consumption of corn.
Still, people have thought that this rise in the money price of corn, by making the crop more profitable to the farmer, must encourage him to grow more of it.

My answer is that this might hold if the bounty raised the real price of corn, so that with the same quantity of it the farmer could support more labourers in the same manner—generous, moderate, or meagre—as labourers are usually supported in his neighbourhood. But clearly neither the bounty nor any other human institution can have such an effect. The bounty can affect only the nominal, not the real, price of corn to any significant degree. And though the tax it lays on the whole population may be a heavy burden to those who pay it, it brings very little benefit to those who receive it.

The real effect of the bounty is not so much to raise the real value of corn as to lower the real value of silver—to make a given quantity of silver exchange for a smaller quantity not only of corn but of every other home-made commodity. For the money price of corn governs that of all other home-made goods.

It governs the money price of labour, which must always be high enough to let the labourer buy enough corn to keep himself and his family—in the generous, moderate, or meagre manner that the advancing, stationary, or declining state of society forces his employers to maintain him.

It governs the money price of all the other raw products of the land, which in every stage of improvement must bear a fixed proportion to the price of corn, though that proportion differs from one stage to another. It governs, for instance, the money price of grass and hay, of butcher's meat, of horses and their upkeep, and so of overland transport—and thus of most of the country's internal commerce.

By governing the money price of all the other raw products of the land, it governs that of the materials of almost every manufacture. By governing the money price of labour, it governs that of manufacturing skill and effort. And by governing both, it governs the price of the finished manufacture. The money price of labour, and of everything produced by land or labour, must necessarily rise or fall in proportion to the money price of corn.

So even if the bounty lets the farmer sell his corn at 4 shillings a bushel instead of 3s 6d, and pay his landlord a money rent in line with this higher money price, it does him little good if, because corn now costs more, those 4 shillings buy no more of any other home-made goods than 3s 6d would have bought before. Neither the farmer's nor the landlord's circumstances improve much by the change. The farmer cannot farm much better; the landlord cannot live much better. On foreign goods this higher corn price may give them some slight advantage. On home-made goods it gives them none at all. And almost all of the farmer's spending, and by far the greater part even of the landlord's, goes on home-made goods.

When the value of silver is lowered by the richness of the mines, and that fall operates equally, or almost equally, across most of the trading world, it matters very little to any one country. The resulting rise in all money prices, though it does not make those who receive the prices truly richer, does not make them truly poorer either. A set of silver plate genuinely becomes cheaper, while everything else keeps exactly the same real value as before.

But when the value of silver is lowered only in one country—because of that country's peculiar situation or political institutions—the matter is very serious, and instead of making anyone truly richer it tends to make everyone truly poorer. The rise in the money price of all goods, peculiar in this case to that one country, tends to discourage every kind of industry carried on within it. It lets foreign nations supply almost every kind of goods for less silver than that country's own workers can manage, and so undersell them not only abroad but even at home.

Spain and Portugal, as owners of the mines, are in the peculiar position of distributing gold and silver to all the other countries of Europe. Those metals ought therefore to be somewhat cheaper in Spain and Portugal than anywhere else in Europe. But the difference should be no more than the cost of freight and insurance; and since these metals carry great value in small bulk, their freight is trifling and their insurance is the same as for any other goods of equal value. So Spain and Portugal would suffer very little from their peculiar situation if they did not make its drawbacks worse through their own political institutions.

Spain by taxing, and Portugal by banning, the export of gold and silver, burden that export with the cost of smuggling, and so raise the value of those metals abroad above their value at home by the full amount of that cost. When you dam up a stream, then as soon as the dam is full, as much water must spill over the top as if there were no dam at all. The export ban cannot keep any more gold and silver in Spain and Portugal than they can put to use—than the annual produce of their land and labour allows them to use in coin, plate, gilding, and other gold and silver ornaments. Once they have that quantity, the dam is full, and the whole inflow that follows must spill over. Accordingly, by all accounts, the annual export of gold and silver from Spain and Portugal, despite these restraints, comes very near to equalling the whole annual import. But just as the water must always stand deeper behind the dam than in front of it, so the quantity of gold and silver these restraints keep in Spain and Portugal must, relative to the annual produce of their land and labour, be greater than what is found in other countries. The higher and stronger the dam, the greater the difference in the depth of water behind and before it. The higher the tax, the harsher the penalties guarding the ban, the more vigilant and severe the policing of the law, the greater the difference in the ratio of gold and silver to the annual produce of land and labour between Spain and Portugal and other countries. That difference is said to be very large, so that one often finds there a lavish display of plate in houses where there is nothing else that in other countries would be thought to match such magnificence. The cheapness of gold and silver—which is the same thing as the dearness of all goods—is the inevitable result of this glut of precious metals, and it discourages both the farming and the manufactures of Spain and Portugal. It lets foreign nations supply them with many kinds of raw produce and almost every kind of manufactured produce for less gold and silver than they can grow or make it for at home. The tax and the ban work in two ways at once. They not only greatly lower the value of the precious metals within Spain and Portugal, but, by holding back there a certain quantity of those metals that would otherwise flow abroad, they prop up the value of the metals in other countries somewhat above what it would otherwise be—and so give those countries a double advantage in their trade with Spain and Portugal. Open the floodgates, and there will soon be less water above and more below the dam, and the level will soon equalize on both sides. Remove the tax and the ban, and as the quantity of gold and silver falls sharply in Spain and Portugal it will rise somewhat in other countries; and the value of those metals, their ratio to the annual produce of land and labour, will soon reach the same level, or very nearly, everywhere. The loss Spain and Portugal might suffer from this outflow of their gold and silver would be wholly nominal and imaginary. The nominal value of their goods, and of the annual produce of their land and labour, would fall, expressed in a smaller quantity of silver than before; but their real value would be the same, and would still maintain, command, and employ the same quantity of labour. As the nominal value of their goods fell, the real value of the gold and silver they had left would rise, and a smaller quantity of those metals would serve all the same purposes of commerce and circulation that a larger quantity had served before. The gold and silver that went abroad would not go for nothing, but would bring back an equal value of goods of one kind or another. Nor would all those goods be mere luxuries and indulgences to be consumed by idle people who produce nothing in return. Since the real wealth and revenue of idle people would not be increased by this extraordinary outflow of gold and silver, neither would their consumption be much increased by it. Most of those goods, and certainly some of them, would consist of materials, tools, and provisions for employing and maintaining industrious people, who would reproduce, at a profit, the full value of what they consumed. Part of the country's dead stock would thus be turned into active stock and would set in motion a greater quantity of industry than before. The annual produce of their land and labour would immediately grow a little, and within a few years would probably grow a great deal, with their industry relieved of one of the heaviest burdens it now labours under.

The bounty on corn exports works in exactly the same way as this absurd policy of Spain and Portugal. Whatever the actual state of farming, it makes our corn somewhat dearer in the home market than it would otherwise be, and somewhat cheaper in the foreign market; and since the average money price of corn governs, more or less, that of all other goods, it lowers the value of silver considerably in the home market and tends to raise it a little abroad. It lets foreigners—the Dutch in particular—not only eat our corn more cheaply than they otherwise could, but sometimes eat it more cheaply than even our own people can on the same occasions, as we are assured by an excellent authority, Sir Matthew Decker. It stops our own workers from supplying their goods for as little silver as they otherwise might, while letting the Dutch supply theirs for less. It tends to make our manufactures somewhat dearer in every market and theirs somewhat cheaper than they would otherwise be, and so gives their industry a double advantage over ours.

Since the bounty raises in the home market not so much the real as the nominal price of our corn—since it increases not the quantity of labour a given quantity of corn can maintain and employ, but only the quantity of silver it will exchange for—it discourages our manufactures without doing any real service to our farmers or country gentlemen. True, it puts a little more money in the pockets of both, and it will perhaps be hard to convince most of them that this is not a very real service. But if that money loses as much in value—in the quantity of labour, provisions, and home-made goods of every kind it can buy—as it gains in quantity, the service will be little more than nominal and imaginary.

There is perhaps only one set of men in the whole nation to whom the bounty either was, or could be, of any real use: the corn merchants, the men who export and import corn. In years of plenty the bounty necessarily caused more exporting than would otherwise have taken place; and by stopping one year's plenty from relieving another year's scarcity, it caused, in years of scarcity, more importing than would otherwise have been needed. It increased the corn merchant's business in both kinds of year; and in years of scarcity it let him not only import a larger quantity, but sell it at a better price, and so with a greater profit, than he could otherwise have made had one year's plenty not been more or less prevented from relieving another year's scarcity. It is among these men, accordingly, that I have noticed the greatest zeal for keeping the bounty going or renewing it.

When our country gentlemen imposed the heavy duties on imported foreign corn—duties that in times of moderate plenty amount to a ban—and when they set up the bounty, they seem to have copied the conduct of our manufacturers. By the first measure they secured for themselves a monopoly of the home market, and by the second they tried to keep that market from ever being overstocked with their commodity. By both they tried to raise its real value, just as our manufacturers had, by similar measures, raised the real value of many kinds of manufactured goods. But they probably failed to notice the great and essential difference nature has set between corn and almost every other kind of goods. When, by a monopoly of the home market or by an export bounty, you let our woollen or linen manufacturers sell their goods for somewhat more than they could otherwise get, you raise not just the nominal but the real price of those goods; you make them equivalent to a greater quantity of labour and subsistence; you increase not just the nominal but the real profit, the real wealth and revenue, of those manufacturers; and you enable them either to live better themselves or to employ more labour in those particular manufactures. You genuinely encourage those manufactures and steer towards them a larger share of the country's industry than would naturally go to them. But when you raise the nominal or money price of corn by similar measures, you do not raise its real value; you do not increase the real wealth or real revenue of our farmers or country gentlemen; you do not encourage the growing of corn, because you do not enable them to maintain and employ more labourers in raising it. Nature has stamped on corn a real value that cannot be altered merely by altering its money price. No export bounty, no home-market monopoly, can raise that value. The freest competition cannot lower it. Across the world in general, that value equals the quantity of labour the corn can maintain; and in any particular place it equals the quantity of labour the corn can maintain in the manner—generous, moderate, or meagre—in which labour is usually maintained there. Woollen or linen cloth are not the standard goods by which the real value of all other goods is ultimately measured and fixed; corn is. The real value of every other commodity is finally measured and fixed by the ratio of its average money price to the average money price of corn. The real value of corn does not change with those swings in its average money price that sometimes occur from one century to another; it is the real value of silver that changes with them.

Bounties on the export of any home-made commodity are open, first, to the general objection that can be made to all the various devices of the mercantile system: the objection that they force part of a country's industry into a channel less advantageous than the one it would naturally take. And second, they are open to the particular objection that they force it not merely into a less advantageous channel but into a positively harmful one, since a trade that can be carried on only by means of a bounty is necessarily a losing trade. The corn-export bounty is open to the further objection that it can in no way promote the growing of the very crop it was meant to encourage. So when our country gentlemen demanded that the bounty be set up, although they were imitating our merchants and manufacturers, they did not act with the full grasp of their own interest that usually guides those two other groups. They loaded the public revenue with a very large expense; they laid a very heavy tax on the whole population; but they did not, to any noticeable degree, raise the real value of their own commodity; and by lowering somewhat the real value of silver, they discouraged the general industry of the country to some degree, and so, instead of advancing, more or less held back the improvement of their own lands, which depend on the general industry of the country.

To encourage the production of any commodity, you would think a bounty on production would work more directly than one on export. It would also impose only one tax on the people, the one they must pay to fund the bounty. Instead of raising the home price of the commodity, it would tend to lower it, and so, instead of laying a second tax on the people, it might at least partly repay them for what they paid towards the first. Yet production bounties have very rarely been granted. The prejudices built up by the commercial system have taught us to believe that national wealth springs more directly from exporting than from producing. Exporting has therefore been the more favoured, as the more immediate way of bringing money into the country. It has also been said that production bounties have proved more open to fraud than export bounties. How true that is, I do not know. That export bounties have been abused for many fraudulent purposes is very well known. But it is not in the interest of the merchants and manufacturers—the great inventors of all these devices—for the home market to be overstocked with their goods, which a production bounty might sometimes bring about. An export bounty, by letting them send their surplus abroad and hold up the price of what remains at home, effectively prevents this. Of all the devices of the mercantile system, the export bounty is accordingly the one they are fondest of. I have known the various undertakers of some particular works privately agree among themselves to pay a bounty out of their own pockets on the export of a certain share of the goods they dealt in. This scheme worked so well that it more than doubled the home-market price of their goods, despite a very large increase in production. The bounty on corn must have worked wonderfully differently if it has actually lowered the money price of that commodity.

Something like a production bounty has, however, been granted on certain occasions. The tonnage bounties given to the white-herring and whale fisheries may perhaps be regarded as somewhat of this kind. They presumably tend directly to make the goods cheaper in the home market than they otherwise would be. In other respects, though, their effects must be admitted to be the same as those of export bounties. Through them, part of the country's capital is used to bring to market goods whose price does not cover the cost plus the ordinary profit on capital.

But although the tonnage bounties to those fisheries do not add to the nation's wealth, it may perhaps be thought that they add to its defence, by increasing the number of its sailors and ships. This, it may be argued, can sometimes be done by such bounties at a far smaller cost than by keeping up a great standing navy, if I may use the phrase, in the same way as a standing army.
Despite these favourable arguments, however, the following considerations incline me to believe that, in granting at least one of these bounties, the legislature has been very badly deceived:
First, the herring-buss bounty seems too large.

From the start of the winter fishery of 1771 to the end of the winter fishery of 1781, the tonnage bounty on the herring-buss fishery stood at thirty shillings a ton. Over those eleven years the Scottish herring-buss fishery caught 378,347 barrels in all. Herrings caught and cured at sea are called sea-sticks. To turn them into what are called merchantable herrings, they must be repacked with extra salt; and in this case it is reckoned that three barrels of sea-sticks usually repack into two barrels of merchantable herrings. So the number of barrels of merchantable herrings caught over those eleven years comes, on this reckoning, to only 252,231¼. Over those eleven years the tonnage bounties paid amounted to £155,463 11s, which works out to 8s 2¼d on every barrel of sea-sticks and 12s 3¾d on every barrel of merchantable herrings.

The salt used to cure these herrings is sometimes Scottish and sometimes foreign, and both are delivered to the fish-curers free of all excise duty. The excise duty is at present 1s 6d on Scottish salt and 10s a bushel on foreign salt. A barrel of herrings is supposed to need about one and a quarter bushels of foreign salt, or, taking Scottish salt, an average of two bushels. If the herrings are entered for export, none of this duty is paid; if entered for home consumption, then whether they were cured with foreign or Scottish salt only one shilling a barrel is paid. That was the old Scottish duty on a bushel of salt, the quantity which, at a low estimate, was supposed to be needed to cure a barrel of herrings. In Scotland foreign salt is used for almost nothing but curing fish. Yet from 5 April 1771 to 5 April 1782 the foreign salt imported came to 936,974 bushels at eighty-four pounds a bushel, while the Scottish salt delivered from the works to the fish-curers came to no more than 168,226 bushels at only fifty-six pounds a bushel. So it appears that the fisheries mainly use foreign salt. On top of all this, every barrel of herrings exported carries a further bounty of 2s 8d, and more than two-thirds of the buss-caught herrings are exported. Put all this together and you find that, over those eleven years, every barrel of buss-caught herrings cured with Scottish salt cost the government 17s 11¾d when exported and 14s 3¾d when entered for home consumption; and that every barrel cured with foreign salt cost the government £1 7s 5¾d when exported and £1 3s 9¾d when entered for home consumption. The price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings runs from seventeen or eighteen to twenty-four or twenty-five shillings, about a guinea on average. (See the accounts at the end of this Book.)

Second, the bounty to the white-herring fishery is a tonnage bounty, tied to the ship's tonnage rather than to her diligence or success at fishing; and I am afraid it has been all too common for vessels to fit out for the sole purpose of catching not the fish but the bounty. In 1759, when the bounty stood at fifty shillings a ton, the whole buss fishery of Scotland brought in only four barrels of sea-sticks. That year each barrel of sea-sticks cost the government, in bounties alone, £113 15s; each barrel of merchantable herrings, £159 7s 6d.

Third, the kind of fishing for which this tonnage bounty in the white-herring fishery has been given—busses, or decked vessels of twenty to eighty tons—seems not as well suited to Scotland's situation as to Holland's, from whose practice it appears to have been copied. Holland lies far from the seas where herrings are known mainly to gather, and so can carry on that fishery only in decked vessels able to hold enough water and provisions for a voyage to a distant sea. But the Hebrides or Western Islands, the Shetland Islands, and the northern and north-western coasts of Scotland—the regions near which the herring fishery is mainly carried on—are everywhere cut by arms of the sea that run a good way inland and that in the local language are called sea-lochs. It is to these sea-lochs that the herrings mainly come during the seasons when they visit these waters; for the visits of this fish, and, I am assured, of many other kinds, are not quite regular and constant. A boat fishery, then, seems to be the kind of fishing best suited to Scotland's particular situation, with the fishers carrying the herrings ashore as fast as they are caught, to be either cured or eaten fresh. But the great encouragement that a bounty of 30s a ton gives to the buss fishery is necessarily a discouragement to the boat fishery, which, having no such bounty, cannot bring its cured fish to market on the same terms as the buss fishery. The boat fishery, accordingly, which before the buss bounty was very considerable and is said to have employed as many seamen as the buss fishery now does, has now almost entirely decayed. As for the former extent of this now ruined and abandoned fishery, I must admit I cannot claim to speak with much precision. Since no bounty was paid on fitting out a boat fishery, the customs or salt-duty officers kept no account of it.

Fourth, in many parts of Scotland, during certain seasons, herrings make up no small part of the common people's food. A bounty that lowered their price in the home market might do a good deal to relieve a great many of our fellow subjects whose circumstances are far from comfortable. But the herring-buss bounty does no such good. It has ruined the boat fishery, by far the best suited to supplying the home market; and the extra export bounty of 2s 8d a barrel carries most of the buss fishery's catch—more than two-thirds of it—abroad. Thirty or forty years ago, before the buss bounty was set up, the common price of white herrings was, I am assured, 16s a barrel. Ten or fifteen years ago, before the boat fishery was wholly ruined, the price was said to run from seventeen to twenty shillings a barrel. For the last five years it has averaged twenty-five shillings a barrel. This high price, however, may be owing to a real scarcity of herrings off the Scottish coast. I must also note that the cask or barrel usually sold with the herrings, whose price is included in all the figures above, has, since the start of the American war, risen to about double its former price, from about 3s to about 6s. And I must note too that the accounts I have received of prices in former times have been by no means quite consistent; an old man of great accuracy and experience has assured me that more than fifty years ago a guinea was the usual price of a barrel of good merchantable herrings, and this, I imagine, may still be taken as the average price. All accounts, however, agree, I think, that the buss bounty has not lowered the price in the home market.

When the undertakers of fisheries, after such generous bounties have been heaped on them, keep selling their commodity at the same or even a higher price than before, you might expect their profits to be very large; and it is not unlikely that some individuals' profits have been so. In general, though, I have every reason to believe the opposite. The usual effect of such bounties is to tempt rash undertakers into a business they do not understand; and what they lose through their own carelessness and ignorance more than wipes out everything they can gain from the utmost generosity of government. In 1750, the same Act that first gave the bounty of 30s a ton to encourage the white-herring fishery (23 Geo. II, ch. 24) set up a joint-stock company with a capital of £500,000. Over and above all the other encouragements—the tonnage bounty just mentioned, the export bounty of 2s 8d a barrel, and the delivery of both British and foreign salt duty-free—the subscribers were entitled, for fourteen years, to three pounds a year for every hundred pounds they subscribed and paid into the company's stock, paid in equal half-yearly instalments by the receiver-general of the customs. Besides this great company, whose governor and directors were to reside in London, it was declared lawful to set up separate fishing chambers in all the kingdom's out-ports, provided a sum of at least £10,000 was subscribed to each, to be run at its own risk and for its own profit and loss. The same annuity and the same encouragements of every kind were given to these lesser chambers as to the great company. The great company's subscription was soon filled, and several fishing chambers were set up in the kingdom's various out-ports. Despite all these encouragements, almost all those companies, great and small, lost either all or most of their capital; scarcely a trace of any of them now remains, and the white-herring fishery is now carried on entirely, or almost entirely, by private adventurers.

If some particular manufacture really were necessary for the defence of the country, it might not always be wise to rely on our neighbours to supply it; and if such a manufacture could not otherwise be kept up at home, it might not be unreasonable to tax all the other branches of industry to support it. The bounties on the export of British-made sail-cloth and British-made gunpowder may perhaps both be defended on this principle.

But although it can very seldom be reasonable to tax the industry of the great body of the people in order to support that of some particular class of manufacturers, yet in the recklessness of great prosperity, when the public enjoys more revenue than it knows what to do with, granting such bounties to favoured manufactures may perhaps be as natural as any other piece of idle spending. In public spending, as in private, great wealth may perhaps often serve as an excuse for great folly. But there must surely be something more than ordinary absurdity in keeping up such extravagance in times of general difficulty and distress.

What is called a bounty is sometimes no more than a drawback, and so is not open to the same objections as a true bounty. The bounty on exported refined sugar, for example, may be regarded as a drawback of the duties on the brown and Muscovado sugars from which it is made; the bounty on exported wrought silk, as a drawback of the duties on imported raw and thrown silk; the bounty on exported gunpowder, as a drawback of the duties on imported brimstone and saltpetre. In the language of the customs, only those allowances are called drawbacks which are given on goods exported in the same form in which they were imported. When that form has been so changed by manufacture as to fall under a new name, they are called bounties.

Premiums given by the public to artists and manufacturers who excel in their particular trades are not open to the same objections as bounties. By encouraging exceptional skill and ingenuity, they help keep up the rivalry among the workers actually employed in those trades, and are not large enough to draw towards any one of them a greater share of the country's capital than would go to it naturally. Their tendency is not to upset the natural balance of employments, but to make the work done in each as perfect and complete as possible. Premiums, besides, cost very little, while bounties cost a great deal. The bounty on corn alone has sometimes cost the public, in a single year, more than £300,000.
Bounties are sometimes called premiums, just as drawbacks are sometimes called bounties. But in every case we must attend to the nature of the thing, with no regard to the word used for it.
A Digression on the Corn Trade and the Corn Laws

I cannot end this chapter on bounties without remarking that the praises lavished on the law that established the bounty on corn exports, and on the system of regulations bound up with it, are wholly undeserved. A close examination of the nature of the corn trade and of the chief British laws relating to it will sufficiently prove this. The great importance of the subject must excuse the length of the digression.

The trade of the corn merchant is made up of four different branches which, though one person may sometimes carry on all of them, are by their nature four separate and distinct trades. These are, first, the trade of the inland dealer; second, that of the merchant who imports for home consumption; third, that of the merchant who exports home produce for foreign consumption; and fourth, that of the merchant-carrier, who imports corn in order to export it again.

I. The interest of the inland dealer and that of the great body of the people, however opposed they may seem at first, are in fact exactly the same, even in years of the greatest scarcity. It is in his interest to raise the price of his corn as high as the real scarcity of the season requires, and never in his interest to raise it any higher. By raising the price he discourages consumption and pushes everyone, especially the lower ranks, towards thrift and good management. If by raising it too high he discourages consumption so much that the season's supply is likely to outlast the season's consumption and run on for some time after the next crop begins to come in, he risks not only losing a good deal of his corn to natural decay but having to sell what remains for far less than he could have got for it several months earlier. If by not raising the price high enough he discourages consumption so little that the season's supply is likely to fall short of the season's consumption, he not only loses part of the profit he might have made but exposes the people, before the season ends, not merely to the hardships of a dearth but to the dreadful horrors of a famine. It is in the people's interest that their daily, weekly, and monthly consumption be matched as exactly as possible to the season's supply. The inland corn dealer's interest is the same. By supplying them, as nearly as he can judge, in that proportion, he is likely to sell all his corn at the highest price and with the greatest profit; and his knowledge of the state of the crop and of his own daily, weekly, and monthly sales lets him judge, more or less accurately, how nearly they are in fact supplied in this way. Without intending the people's good, he is necessarily led, by regard for his own interest, to treat them, even in years of scarcity, much as a prudent ship's master sometimes has to treat his crew. When he foresees that provisions are likely to run short, he puts them on short rations. Though out of excess of caution he may sometimes do this without real need, all the inconvenience his crew can suffer from it is trifling compared with the danger, misery, and ruin to which a less provident course might sometimes expose them. In the same way, though out of excess of greed the inland corn merchant may sometimes raise his price somewhat higher than the season's scarcity requires, all the inconvenience the people can suffer from his conduct—which effectively saves them from famine at the season's end—is trifling compared with what they might have faced from a more lavish way of dealing at its start. And the corn merchant himself is likely to suffer most from this excess of greed: not only from the general indignation it stirs up against him, but, even if he escapes that, from the quantity of corn it necessarily leaves on his hands at the season's end, which, if the next season proves good, he must always sell for far less than he might otherwise have got.

If it really were possible for one great company of merchants to get hold of the whole crop of an extensive country, it might perhaps be in their interest to treat it as the Dutch are said to treat the spices of the Moluccas—to destroy or throw away a large part of it in order to keep up the price of the rest. But it is hardly possible, even by the force of law, to set up so wide a monopoly over corn; and wherever the law leaves the trade free, corn is of all commodities the least liable to be cornered or monopolized by the power of a few large capitals buying up the greater part of it. Not only does its total value far exceed what a few private men's capitals could buy; but even supposing they could afford to buy it, the way it is produced makes such a purchase quite impossible. In every civilized country corn is the commodity whose annual consumption is greatest, so a greater quantity of industry is employed each year in producing it than in producing any other commodity. When it first comes from the ground, too, it is necessarily divided among more owners than any other commodity; and these owners can never be gathered into one place, like a body of independent manufacturers, but are necessarily scattered through every corner of the country. These first owners either supply consumers in their own neighbourhood directly, or supply other inland dealers who supply those consumers. So the inland dealers in corn—including both the farmer and the baker—are necessarily more numerous than the dealers in any other commodity, and their scattered situation makes it altogether impossible for them to enter into any general combination. If, in a year of scarcity, any one of them found he had a good deal more corn on hand than he could hope to sell at the current price before the season ended, he would never dream of keeping the price up to his own loss and the sole benefit of his rivals, but would lower it at once to get rid of his corn before the new crop began to come in. The same motives and the same interests that would govern any one dealer would govern every other, and would oblige them all to sell their corn at the price which, by their best judgment, was most suited to the scarcity or plenty of the season.

Anyone who studies, with attention, the history of the dearths and famines that have afflicted any part of Europe in either this century or the two before it—of several of which we have fairly exact accounts—will find, I believe, that a dearth has never arisen from any combination among the inland dealers in corn, nor from any cause but a real scarcity, occasioned sometimes, perhaps, in particular places, by the ravages of war, but in the great majority of cases by the fault of the seasons; and that a famine has never arisen from any cause but the violence of a government trying, by improper means, to remedy the troubles of a dearth.

In an extensive corn-growing country with free trade and communication among all its parts, the scarcity caused by the worst seasons can never be great enough to produce a famine; and the scantiest crop, if managed with frugality and economy, will feed through the year the same number of people who are normally fed more amply by a crop of moderate plenty. The seasons most harmful to the crop are those of excessive drought or excessive rain. But since corn grows alike on high and low ground, on land inclined to be too wet and on land inclined to be too dry, the drought or rain that hurts one part of the country helps another; and though in both wet and dry seasons the crop is a good deal smaller than in one better balanced, yet in both, what is lost in one part of the country is to some extent made up by what is gained in another. In rice-growing countries, where the crop not only needs a very moist soil but must at a certain stage of its growth be kept under water, the effects of a drought are far more dreadful. Even there, however, a drought is perhaps hardly ever so universal as to bring on a famine, if the government would allow free trade. The drought in Bengal a few years ago might well have caused a very great dearth. Some improper regulations, some misguided restraints, imposed by the servants of the East India Company on the rice trade, perhaps helped turn that dearth into a famine.

When the government, to remedy the troubles of a dearth, orders all the dealers to sell their corn at what it supposes a reasonable price, it either stops them from bringing it to market—which may sometimes produce a famine even at the start of the season—or, if they do bring it, it enables, and so encourages, the people to consume it so fast that famine must necessarily follow before the season ends. The unlimited, unrestrained freedom of the corn trade is the only effective preventive of the miseries of famine, and it is also the best palliative of the troubles of a dearth; for the troubles of a real scarcity cannot be cured, only eased. No trade deserves the full protection of the law more, and none needs it so much, because no trade is so exposed to popular hatred.

In years of scarcity, the lower ranks of people blame their hardship on the greed of the corn merchant, who becomes the target of their hatred and outrage. So instead of profiting at such times, he often risks being completely ruined, with his warehouses looted and wrecked by their violence. Yet it is precisely in scarce years, when prices are high, that the corn merchant expects to make his main profit. He usually has contracts with certain farmers to supply him, over a fixed number of years, with a fixed quantity of corn at a fixed price. That contract price is set by what is thought to be the moderate and reasonable level—that is, the ordinary or average price—which, before the recent years of scarcity, was commonly around 28s. for a quarter of wheat, and proportionally for other grain. In scarce years, then, the corn merchant buys much of his corn at the ordinary price and sells it for much more. But that this extra profit is only enough to put his trade on a fair footing with other trades, and to make up for the many losses he suffers at other times—both from the perishable nature of the goods themselves and from the frequent, unpredictable swings in their price—seems clear enough from one fact: great fortunes are as rarely made in this trade as in any other. The public hatred that follows it in scarce years, the only years when it can be very profitable, keeps people of standing and wealth from entering it. It is left to an inferior class of dealers; and millers, bakers, meal-men, and meal-factors, along with a crowd of wretched hucksters, are almost the only middlemen who, in the home market, stand between the grower and the consumer.
The old policy of Europe, far from discouraging this public hatred toward a trade so useful to the public, seems on the contrary to have sanctioned and encouraged it.

The Act of the 5th and 6th of Edward VI, chapter 14, declared that anyone who bought corn or grain meaning to sell it again should be treated as an unlawful engrosser. For a first offence he was to be imprisoned for two months and forfeit the value of the corn; for a second, imprisoned for six months and forfeit double the value; and for a third, set in the pillory, imprisoned at the king's pleasure, and stripped of all his goods and possessions. The old policy of most other parts of Europe was no better than England's.

Our ancestors seem to have supposed that people would buy their corn more cheaply from the farmer than from the corn merchant, whom they feared would demand, on top of the price he paid the farmer, an excessive profit for himself. So they tried to wipe out his trade entirely. They even tried to keep any middleman of any sort, as far as possible, from coming between the grower and the consumer; and that was the point of the many restraints they placed on the trade of those they called kidders, or carriers of corn—a trade no one was allowed to practise without a licence confirming that he was a man of honesty and fair dealing. By Edward VI's statute, the authority of three justices of the peace was needed to grant this licence. But even this restraint was later judged too weak, and by a statute of Elizabeth the power to grant it was limited to the quarter-sessions.

In this way the old policy of Europe tried to regulate agriculture, the great trade of the countryside, by rules quite different from those it set for manufactures, the great trade of the towns. By leaving the farmer no customers except either the consumers themselves or their immediate agents, the kidders and carriers of corn, it forced him to act not only as a farmer but as a corn merchant or corn retailer too. With manufacturers it did the opposite: in many cases it forbade them from acting as shopkeepers or from selling their own goods by retail. By the first law it meant to serve the general interest of the country, or to make corn cheap, though perhaps without anyone clearly understanding how that was to be achieved. By the second it meant to serve the interest of one particular group of men, the shopkeepers, who were assumed to be so heavily undersold by the manufacturer that their trade would be ruined if he were allowed to retail at all.

In fact, even if the manufacturer had been permitted to keep a shop and sell his own goods by retail, he could not have undersold the ordinary shopkeeper. Whatever part of his capital he put into his shop, he would have had to withdraw from his manufacturing. To run his business on the same footing as everyone else, he would need the profit of a manufacturer on one side and the profit of a shopkeeper on the other. Suppose, for instance, that in his particular town ten per cent was the ordinary profit on both manufacturing and shopkeeping stock; he would then have had to charge a profit of twenty per cent on every piece of his own goods that he sold in his shop. When he moved them from his workshop to his shop, he had to value them at the price he could have got from a dealer or shopkeeper buying wholesale. If he valued them lower, he lost part of the profit on his manufacturing capital. And when he sold them from his shop, unless he got the same price a shopkeeper would have charged, he lost part of the profit on his shopkeeping capital. So although he might seem to make a double profit on the same piece of goods, in fact, since those goods were in turn part of two separate capitals, he made only a single profit on the whole capital tied up in them; and if he made less than that, he was a loser and did not employ his whole capital as advantageously as most of his neighbours did.

What the manufacturer was forbidden to do, the farmer was in a sense ordered to do: to split his capital between two different uses, keeping one part in his granaries and stack-yard to meet the market's occasional demands, and putting the other into cultivating his land. But just as he could not afford to use the second part for less than the ordinary profits of farming stock, so he could just as little afford to use the first for less than the ordinary profits of mercantile stock. Whether the capital that actually carried on the corn merchant's business belonged to the man called a farmer or to the man called a corn merchant, an equal profit was needed in either case—to compensate the owner for employing it this way, to put his business on the same footing as other trades, and to remove any incentive to switch it for some other trade as soon as he could. So the farmer who was forced to act as a corn merchant could not afford to sell his corn any cheaper than any other corn merchant would have had to in a state of free competition.

The dealer who can put his whole stock into a single line of business has the same kind of advantage as the workman who can put all his labour into a single operation. Just as the workman gains a dexterity that lets him, with the same two hands, do far more work, so the dealer gains so quick and easy a way of conducting his business—of buying and disposing of his goods—that with the same capital he can handle far more business. And just as the one can usually supply his work a good deal cheaper, so the other can usually supply his goods somewhat cheaper, than if his stock and attention were spread across a greater variety of things. Most manufacturers could not afford to retail their own goods as cheaply as an alert, active shopkeeper whose only business was to buy them wholesale and retail them again. And most farmers could afford it even less—to retail their own corn, supplying the people of a town perhaps four or five miles from most of them, as cheaply as an alert, active corn merchant whose only business was to buy corn wholesale, gather it into a large warehouse, and retail it again.

The law that barred the manufacturer from acting as a shopkeeper tried to push this division in the use of capital along faster than it might otherwise have gone. The law that compelled the farmer to act as a corn merchant tried to hold it back. Both laws plainly violated natural liberty, and were therefore unjust; and both were as foolish as they were unjust. It is in every society's interest that matters of this kind should never be either forced or obstructed. The man who spreads his labour or his capital across more lines than his situation requires can never harm his neighbour by underselling him. He may harm himself, and generally does. Jack-of-all-trades will never be rich, says the proverb. The law should always trust people to look after their own interest, since in their own local circumstances they are generally better judges of it than the legislature can be. The law that compelled the farmer to act as a corn merchant, however, was by far the more harmful of the two.

It obstructed not only that division in the use of capital which is so beneficial to every society, but also the improvement and cultivation of the land. By forcing the farmer to run two trades instead of one, it made him split his capital into two parts, only one of which could go into cultivation. Had he been free instead to sell his whole crop to a corn merchant as fast as he could thresh it, his whole capital could have flowed straight back into the land, going to buy more cattle and hire more servants so as to improve and cultivate it better. But being obliged to retail his corn, he had to keep much of his capital in his granaries and stack-yard throughout the year, and so could not cultivate as well as the same capital might otherwise have let him. This law, then, was bound to obstruct the improvement of the land, and instead of tending to make corn cheaper, it must have tended to make it scarcer—and therefore dearer—than it would otherwise have been.

After the farmer's business, the corn merchant's is really the trade that, if properly protected and encouraged, would do most to increase the supply of corn. It would support the farmer's trade in the same way that the wholesale dealer's trade supports that of the manufacturer.

By providing the manufacturer with a ready market—taking his goods off his hands as fast as he can make them, and sometimes even paying for them before they are made—the wholesale dealer lets him keep his whole capital, and sometimes even more than his whole capital, constantly busy in manufacturing, and so to produce far more goods than if he had to dispose of them himself to the consumers directly, or even to the retailers. And since the wholesale merchant's capital is generally large enough to replace that of many manufacturers, this exchange between him and them gives the owner of a large capital an interest in supporting the owners of many small ones, and in helping them through the losses and misfortunes that might otherwise ruin them.

An exchange of the same kind, established universally between farmers and corn merchants, would bring effects just as beneficial to the farmers. They would be able to keep their whole capitals, and even more than their whole capitals, constantly busy in cultivation. When hit by any of those accidents to which no trade is more exposed than theirs, they would find in their regular customer, the wealthy corn merchant, someone with both an interest in supporting them and the means to do it; and they would not, as now, be left entirely dependent on the forbearance of their landlord or the mercy of his steward. If it were possible—as perhaps it is not—to set up this exchange everywhere and all at once; if it were possible to turn the whole farming stock of the kingdom all at once to its proper task, the cultivation of land, withdrawing it from every other use into which part of it may now be diverted; and if it were possible, in order to support and assist this great stock when needed, to provide all at once another stock almost as large; then it is not easy to imagine how great, how widespread, and how sudden the improvement would be that this change of circumstances alone would bring to the whole face of the country.

So the statute of Edward VI, by barring middlemen as far as possible from coming between the grower and the consumer, tried to wipe out a trade whose free practice is not only the best remedy for the hardships of a dearth but the best safeguard against that calamity—since, after the farmer's trade, none does so much to grow corn as the corn merchant's.

The harshness of this law was later softened by several successive statutes, which one after another allowed the engrossing of corn whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 20s., then 24s., 32s., and 40s. the quarter. Finally, by the 15th of Charles II, chapter 7, engrossing or buying corn in order to sell it again was declared lawful for anyone who was not a forestaller—that is, who did not resell in the same market within three months—so long as the price of wheat did not exceed 48s. the quarter, and that of other grain proportionally. All the freedom the inland corn trade has ever enjoyed was granted to it by this statute. The statute of the twelfth year of the present king, which repeals almost all the other old laws against engrossers and forestallers, does not repeal the restrictions of this particular statute, which therefore remain in force.
This statute, however, lends some support to two very absurd popular prejudices.

First, it assumes that once the price of wheat has risen as high as 48s. the quarter, with other grain in proportion, corn is likely to be engrossed enough to hurt the people. But from what has already been said it seems clear enough that corn can at no price be so engrossed by inland dealers as to hurt the people; and besides, 48s. the quarter, though it may count as a very high price, is in scarce years a price that often occurs right after harvest, when hardly any of the new crop can yet have been sold off, and when not even ignorance could suppose that any part of it has been engrossed enough to hurt the people.

Second, it assumes there is a certain price at which corn is likely to be forestalled—that is, bought up to be resold soon after in the same market—so as to hurt the people. But if a merchant ever does buy up corn, whether on its way to a particular market or in that market, in order to resell it soon after in the same market, it must be because he judges that the market cannot be as well supplied through the whole season as it is on that particular occasion, and that the price must therefore soon rise. If he judges wrong and the price does not rise, he loses not only the whole profit on the stock he employs this way but part of the stock itself, through the expense and waste that inevitably go with storing and keeping corn. So he hurts himself far more seriously than he can hurt even the particular people he may stop from supplying themselves on that one market day, since they can afterwards supply themselves just as cheaply on any other market day. If he judges right, then far from hurting the great body of the people he does them a most important service. By making them feel the hardships of a dearth somewhat earlier than they otherwise would, he keeps them from feeling them later as severely as they surely would if cheap prices had encouraged them to consume faster than the season's real scarcity allowed. When the scarcity is real, the best thing that can be done for the people is to spread its hardship as evenly as possible across all the different months and weeks and days of the year. The corn merchant's own interest leads him to try to do this as exactly as he can; and since no one else can have the same interest, the same knowledge, or the same ability to do it so precisely, this most important operation of commerce ought to be left entirely to him—in other words, the corn trade, at least so far as it concerns the supply of the home market, ought to be left completely free.

The popular fear of engrossing and forestalling may be compared to the popular terror and suspicion of witchcraft. The unfortunate wretches accused of witchcraft were no more guilty of the misfortunes blamed on them than those accused of engrossing and forestalling. The law that ended all prosecutions for witchcraft, taking away any man's power to indulge his malice by accusing his neighbour of that imaginary crime, seems to have effectively ended those fears and suspicions by removing the great cause that fed and sustained them. A law restoring full freedom to the inland corn trade would probably prove just as effective in ending the popular fear of engrossing and forestalling.

The 15th of Charles II, chapter 7, with all its flaws, has perhaps done more, both for the plentiful supply of the home market and for the growth of tillage, than any other law on the statute book. It is from this law that the inland corn trade has gained all the liberty and protection it has ever yet enjoyed; and both the supply of the home market and the interest of tillage are far more effectively promoted by the inland trade than by either the import or the export trade.

The author of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade has calculated that the average quantity of all kinds of grain imported into Great Britain comes to no more than one part in five hundred and seventy of all the grain consumed. For supplying the home market, then, the importance of the inland trade must be to that of the import trade as five hundred and seventy to one.

According to the same author, the average quantity of all kinds of grain exported from Great Britain comes to no more than a thirty-first part of the annual produce. For encouraging tillage, therefore, by providing a market for the home produce, the importance of the inland trade must be to that of the export trade as thirty to one.

I have no great faith in political arithmetic, and I do not mean to vouch for the exactness of either of these calculations. I mention them only to show how much less important, in the view of the most judicious and experienced people, the foreign corn trade is than the home trade. The great cheapness of corn in the years just before the bounty was set up may perhaps, with reason, be ascribed in part to the working of this statute of Charles II, which had been passed about twenty-five years earlier and had therefore had full time to take effect.
A very few words will be enough to cover all I have to say about the other three branches of the corn trade.

II. The trade of the merchant who imports foreign corn for home consumption plainly adds to the immediate supply of the home market, and so far must be of immediate benefit to the great body of the people. It does tend to lower somewhat the average money price of corn, but not to lessen its real value, or the quantity of labour it can maintain. If importation were always free, our farmers and country gentlemen would probably, taking one year with another, get less money for their corn than they do now, when importation is most of the time effectively banned; but the money they did get would be worth more, would buy more goods of every kind, and would employ more labour. Their real wealth, their real revenue, would therefore be the same as now, though it might be expressed in a smaller quantity of silver, and they would be neither prevented nor discouraged from growing as much corn as they do at present. On the contrary, since the rise in the real value of silver that comes from lowering the money price of corn also lowers somewhat the money price of all other goods, it gives the industry of the country where this happens some advantage in every foreign market, and so tends to encourage and increase that industry. But the size of the home market for corn must be proportional to the general industry of the country where the corn grows—that is, to the number of those who produce something else, and who therefore have something else, or, what comes to the same thing, the price of something else, to give in exchange for corn. And in every country the home market, being the nearest and most convenient, is also the largest and most important market for corn. So that rise in the real value of silver which results from lowering the average money price of corn tends to enlarge the largest and most important market for corn, and thereby to encourage rather than discourage its growth.

By the 22nd of Charles II, chapter 13, whenever the price in the home market did not exceed 53s. 4d. the quarter, the importation of wheat was subject to a duty of 16s. the quarter; and to a duty of 8s. whenever the price did not exceed £4. The first of these two prices has, for more than a century now, occurred only in times of very great scarcity; and the second has, so far as I know, never occurred at all. Yet until wheat rose above this second price it was, by this statute, subject to a very high duty; and until it rose above the first, to a duty that amounted to a prohibition. The importation of other kinds of grain was held back by rates and duties, proportional to the value of the grain, that were almost equally high.
