These different duties were imposed partly by the 22nd of Charles II, replacing the old subsidy, and partly by the new subsidy, by the one-third and two-thirds subsidy, and by the subsidy of 1747. Later laws raised those duties still further.

The distress that, in scarce years, the strict enforcement of these laws might have brought on the people would probably have been very great; but on such occasions their enforcement was generally suspended by temporary statutes that allowed, for a limited time, the importation of foreign corn. The very need for these temporary statutes is proof enough of how improper the general one was.

These restraints on importation, though earlier than the establishment of the bounty, sprang from the same spirit and the same principles that later produced that regulation. However harmful in themselves, these or some other restraints on importation became necessary as a consequence of that regulation. If, when wheat was either below 48s. the quarter or not much above it, foreign corn could have been imported either duty free or on paying only a small duty, it might then have been exported again with the benefit of the bounty—a great loss to the public revenue, and a complete perversion of the scheme, whose aim was to widen the market for home-grown corn, not for corn grown in foreign countries.

III. The trade of the merchant who exports corn for foreign consumption certainly does not add directly to the plentiful supply of the home market. It does so, however, indirectly. Whatever the usual source of that supply—whether home growth or foreign importation—unless more corn is usually grown, or usually imported into the country, than is usually consumed in it, the home market can never be very well supplied. But unless the surplus can normally be exported, growers will be careful never to grow more, and importers never to import more, than the bare consumption of the home market requires. That market will very rarely be overstocked; but it will generally be understocked, since the people whose business it is to supply it are generally afraid of being left with goods on their hands. A ban on exportation confines the improvement and cultivation of the country to what its own inhabitants' consumption requires. Freedom of exportation lets it extend cultivation to supply foreign nations as well.

By the 12th of Charles II, chapter 4, the exportation of corn was allowed whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 40s. the quarter, with other grain in proportion. By the 15th year of the same prince this liberty was extended until the price of wheat exceeded 48s. the quarter; and by the 22nd, to all higher prices. A poundage was indeed to be paid to the king on such exportation; but all grain was rated so low in the book of rates that this poundage came to only 1s. on wheat, 4d. on oats, and 6d. the quarter on all other grain. By the 1st of William and Mary, the act that established the bounty, this small duty was in effect removed whenever the price of wheat did not exceed 48s. the quarter; and by the 11th and 12th of William III, chapter 20, it was expressly removed at all higher prices.

In this way the export merchant's trade was not only encouraged by a bounty but made much freer than that of the inland dealer. By the last of these statutes, corn could be engrossed at any price for export; but it could not be engrossed for inland sale except when the price did not exceed 48s. the quarter. Yet the inland dealer's interest, as already shown, can never run counter to that of the great body of the people. The export merchant's interest may, and in fact sometimes does. If, while his own country is suffering a dearth, a neighbouring country were struck by famine, it might be in his interest to carry corn there in quantities that would greatly worsen the hardship of the dearth at home. The plentiful supply of the home market was not the direct object of those statutes; rather, under the pretence of encouraging agriculture, their aim was to push the money price of corn as high as possible, and so to keep up, as far as possible, a constant dearth in the home market. By discouraging importation, the supply of that market, even in times of great scarcity, was confined to the home growth; and by encouraging exportation once the price reached 48s. the quarter, that market was not allowed, even in times of considerable scarcity, to enjoy the whole of that growth. The temporary laws—banning the exportation of corn for a limited time, and lifting the import duties for a limited time—to which Great Britain has had to resort so often, are proof enough of how improper her general system was. Had that system been sound, she would not have been so frequently forced to depart from it.

If all nations followed the liberal system of free exportation and free importation, the different states into which a great continent was divided would so far resemble the different provinces of a great empire. Among the provinces of a great empire, freedom of inland trade appears, from both reason and experience, not only the best remedy for a dearth but the most effective safeguard against a famine; and so would freedom of the export and import trade be among the different states into which a great continent was divided. The larger the continent, and the easier the communication through all its parts by land and water, the less any one particular part of it would ever be exposed to either calamity, since the scarcity of one country would be more likely to be relieved by the plenty of another. But very few countries have fully adopted this liberal system. The freedom of the corn trade is almost everywhere more or less restrained, and in many countries is hedged in by such absurd regulations as often aggravate the unavoidable misfortune of a dearth into the dreadful calamity of a famine. The demand of such countries for corn may often grow so great and so urgent that a small neighbouring state, which happened at the same time to be suffering some degree of dearth, could not dare to supply them without exposing itself to the same dreadful calamity. The very bad policy of one country may thus make it, to some extent, dangerous and unwise to establish what would otherwise be the best policy in another. The unlimited freedom of exportation, however, would be far less dangerous in great states, where the growth being much larger, the supply could rarely be much affected by any quantity of corn likely to be exported. In a Swiss canton, or in some of the little states of Italy, it may perhaps sometimes be necessary to restrain the exportation of corn. In great countries like France or England, it scarcely ever can be. Besides, to stop the farmer from sending his goods at all times to the best market is plainly to sacrifice the ordinary laws of justice to a notion of public utility, to a kind of reason of state—an act of legislative authority that ought to be used, and can be excused, only in cases of the most urgent necessity. The price at which the exportation of corn is banned, if it is ever to be banned, ought always to be a very high price.

The laws about corn may everywhere be compared to the laws about religion. People feel themselves so deeply concerned in whatever touches either their subsistence in this life or their happiness in the life to come, that government must give way to their prejudices and, in order to keep the public peace, establish the system they approve of. That, perhaps, is why we so rarely find a reasonable system established with regard to either of these two great concerns.

IV. The trade of the merchant-carrier, who imports foreign corn in order to export it again, adds to the plentiful supply of the home market. It is not, admittedly, the direct purpose of his trade to sell his corn there; but he will generally be willing to do so, and even for a good deal less than he might expect in a foreign market, because in this way he saves the cost of loading and unloading, of freight and insurance. The people of a country that, through the carrying trade, becomes the warehouse and storehouse for supplying other countries can very rarely be in want themselves. So although the carrying trade must lower the average money price of corn in the home market, it would not thereby lower its real value; it would only raise somewhat the real value of silver.

The carrying trade was in effect banned in Great Britain on all ordinary occasions by the high duties on the importation of foreign corn, most of which carried no drawback; and on extraordinary occasions, when a scarcity made it necessary to suspend those duties by temporary statutes, exportation was always banned. By this system of laws, therefore, the carrying trade was in effect banned.

That system of laws, then, which is tied to the establishment of the bounty, seems to deserve no share of the praise heaped on it. The improvement and prosperity of Great Britain, so often credited to those laws, can easily be explained by other causes. The security that the laws of Great Britain give every man, that he shall enjoy the fruits of his own labour, is by itself enough to make any country flourish, despite these and twenty other absurd regulations of commerce; and this security was perfected by the Revolution, at about the same time the bounty was established. The natural effort of every individual to better his own condition, when allowed to act with freedom and security, is so powerful a principle that on its own, without any help, it is capable not only of carrying society to wealth and prosperity but of overcoming a hundred impertinent obstructions with which the folly of human laws too often hampers its working—though the effect of those obstructions is always, more or less, either to encroach on its freedom or to lessen its security. In Great Britain industry is perfectly secure; and though it is far from being perfectly free, it is as free as, or freer than, in any other part of Europe.

Though the period of Great Britain's greatest prosperity and improvement has come after the system of laws tied to the bounty, we must not on that account credit it to those laws. It has also come after the national debt; but the national debt has most certainly not been its cause.

Though the system of laws tied to the bounty has exactly the same tendency as the practice of Spain and Portugal—to lower somewhat the value of the precious metals in the country where it operates—Great Britain is certainly one of the richest countries in Europe, while Spain and Portugal are perhaps among the most wretched. This difference of situation, however, is easily explained by two distinct causes. First, the tax in Spain and the ban in Portugal on exporting gold and silver, together with the watchful police that enforces those laws, must, in two very poor countries which between them import upwards of six million sterling a year, work not only more directly but far more forcibly to reduce the value of those metals there than the corn laws can do in Great Britain. And second, this bad policy is not, in those countries, offset by the general liberty and security of the people. There industry is neither free nor secure; and the civil and ecclesiastical governments of both Spain and Portugal are such as would by themselves be enough to perpetuate their present poverty, even if their regulations of commerce were as wise as most of them are absurd and foolish.

The 13th of the present king, chapter 43, seems to have established a new system with regard to the corn laws, in many respects better than the old one, but in one or two respects perhaps not quite so good.

By this statute the high duties on importation for home consumption are removed as soon as the price of middling wheat rises to 48s. the quarter; that of middling rye, pease, or beans to 32s.; that of barley to 24s.; and that of oats to 16s. In their place a small duty is imposed of only 6d. on the quarter of wheat, and on other grain in proportion. For all these different kinds of grain, but particularly for wheat, the home market is thus opened to foreign supplies at prices considerably lower than before.

By the same statute, the old bounty of 5s. on the exportation of wheat ceases as soon as the price rises to 44s. the quarter, instead of the 48s. at which it ceased before; the bounty of 2s. 6d. on the exportation of barley ceases as soon as the price rises to 22s., instead of the 24s. before; and the bounty of 2s. 6d. on the exportation of oatmeal ceases as soon as the price rises to 14s., instead of the 15s. before. The bounty on rye is reduced from 3s. 6d. to 3s., and it ceases as soon as the price rises to 28s., instead of the 32s. before. If bounties are as improper as I have tried to prove them to be, then the sooner they cease and the lower they are, the better.

The same statute permits, at the lowest prices, the importation of corn for re-export, duty free, provided that in the meantime it is kept in a warehouse under the joint locks of the king and the importer. This liberty, however, extends to no more than twenty-five of Great Britain's ports. They are, though, the principal ones; and there may perhaps not be warehouses suitable for this purpose in most of the others.
So far, this law seems clearly an improvement on the old system.

But by the same law a bounty of 2s. the quarter is given for the exportation of oats whenever the price does not exceed fourteen shillings. No bounty had ever been given before for the exportation of this grain, any more than for that of pease or beans.

By the same law, too, the exportation of wheat is banned as soon as the price rises to forty-four shillings the quarter; that of rye as soon as it rises to twenty-eight shillings; that of barley as soon as it rises to twenty-two shillings; and that of oats as soon as they rise to fourteen shillings. All these prices seem a good deal too low; and there seems, besides, to be something improper in banning exportation altogether at the very prices at which the bounty, which was given to force that exportation, is withdrawn. The bounty ought certainly either to have been withdrawn at a much lower price, or exportation to have been allowed at a much higher one.

So far, then, this law seems inferior to the old system. With all its imperfections, however, we may perhaps say of it what was said of the laws of Solon: that though not the best in itself, it is the best that the interests, prejudices, and temper of the times would allow. In time it may perhaps prepare the way for a better one.
